findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: Building for Lewisham Strategic Partner scheme commits £95.8m while completing procurement
findings.detail: The council has included £95.8m for the first schemes (Thomas Lane Yard and Achilles regeneration phases 1-2) dependent on completing a Strategic Partner procurement. This major scheme experienced £11.4m slippage in the previous year.
findings.matters: This represents 12% of the full capital programme committed dependent on completing a procurement. Given the historical slippage on this programme, delivery and funding risk are material for lenders.
findings.figures: £95.8m budget for first schemes; prior year BfL slippage £11.4m (55% of budget)
findings.quote: A key delivery mechanism is the conclusion of the procurement of a Strategic Partner. This has resulted in the inclusion of the programme and the £95.8m budget needed for the first schemes.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: Contingent £775.73m GLA housing grant bid, with £50.99m additional borrowing if approved
findings.detail: The council has bid for £775.73m of affordable housing grant from the GLA to deliver 3,070 homes over 10 years. If successful, this would increase the capital programme by £169.5m over four years and trigger £50.99m additional borrowing. The bid outcome is not yet known and any approval will require Mayor and Cabinet decision.
findings.matters: This massive contingent commitment creates material forecast uncertainty. If the bid succeeds, borrowing increases significantly; if it fails, housing delivery targets may be missed. Lenders need clarity on which scenario is planned for.
findings.figures: £775.73m grant bid pending; potential programme increase £169,516,311 over four years; potential additional borrowing £50,991,293
findings.quote: The Council has put forward an ambitious bid to the GLA for £775.73m of affordable housing grant to deliver 3,070 homes over for the next 10 years. Whilst we are yet to hear the outcome from this... if successful this could increase the programme over the next four years by £169,516,311

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: £10m contingency funded from reserves for urgent risks and pressures
findings.detail: The council has included a £10m contingency budget (split between HRA and general fund) funded from reserves to cover urgent works that preclude formal member approval in advance. Use of this contingency will draw down reserves and be reported to members retrospectively.
findings.matters: Reserve-funded contingencies indicate either incomplete budgeting for known risks or identified-but-unquantified pressures. Drawing reserves to fund contingencies indicates pressure on the council's financial cushion.
findings.figures: £10m contingency budget across HRA and general fund, funded from reserves
findings.quote: The inclusion of a £10m contingency budget into the 2026/27 budget... will ensure that works of an urgent nature can be delivered. The £10m, if needed, will be funded from reserves in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: £293.2m of external borrowing committed across the expanded capital programme
findings.detail: The council is committing £293.2m of prudential borrowing to deliver the current capital programme: £51.5m from the general fund and £241.7m from the HRA. The council states this remains within Treasury Management Strategy tolerances, but represents material debt commitment.
findings.matters: High borrowing levels constrain future financial flexibility and increase debt servicing costs. Lenders need to assess whether debt levels are sustainable and whether there is headroom for additional borrowing if external funding sources fail.
findings.figures: £293.2m total external borrowing (£51.5m general fund; £241.7m HRA)
findings.quote: The agreed budget forecast £293.2m of external borrowing to deliver the current programme, meaning that the decisions within this report would not breach the agreed Treasury Management Strategy (TMS)

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: Capital programme increased by £231.1m (43%) in a single update cycle
findings.detail: The approved capital programme was expanded from £539.3m (March 2026 budget) to £770.3m, a net increase of £231.1m. This includes £95.8m for the Building for Lewisham Strategic Partner schemes and £68m added to future HRA years to align with the 30-year business plan.
findings.matters: A 43% programme expansion in a single update signals either incomplete original planning or significant replanning between March and July. For lenders, this raises questions about forecast accuracy and financial control.
findings.figures: £28.3m increase for 2026/27; £202.7m increase for 2027/28 onward; total net increase £231.1m
findings.quote: Agree that the cumulative impact of all the above recommendations is a net increase of £28.3m for 2026/27 and an increase of £202.7m for 2027/28 onward, totalling a net increase to the full Capital Programme of £231.1m.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: Significant capital programme slippage in 2025/26, particularly in major housing schemes
findings.detail: The council's capital programme outturn was £139.4m against a budget of £178.1m, a £38.7m (21.7%) underspend. The Building for Lewisham HRA programme specifically underperformed by £11.4m (budget £20.8m, outturn £9.4m). The main HRA capital programme (Decent Homes) also slipped by £18.8m.
findings.matters: Large slippage indicates delivery risk on the council's major housing and infrastructure schemes. For lenders, this means timelines for homes delivery, community benefits, infrastructure development, and debt servicing may slip.
findings.figures: £139.4m outturn against £178.1m budget (£38.7m slippage = 21.7%); Building for Lewisham HRA: £9.4m outturn against £20.8m budget (£11.4m shortfall)
findings.quote: This shows an outturn of £139.4m against a budget of £178.1m, indicating a slippage of £38.7m at year end.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme July Council 2026
findings.headline: Council acknowledges risk that capital projects may overspend allocated budgets
findings.detail: The report states that despite project budgets including contingencies, there is a risk of project overspends. If overspends occur, the Council will seek additional budget to cover the shortfall.
findings.matters: Acknowledged risk suggests contingencies may prove insufficient, creating potential for additional funding demands beyond the approved programme.
findings.figures: (none specified)
findings.quote: Although project budgets are usually prudent & include contingencies, there is a risk that projects may overspend their allocated budget. In this scenario, additional budget will need to be sought to fund this overspend.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme July Council 2026
findings.headline: £68m HRA capital budget addition for future years based on updated 30-year business plan
findings.detail: The HRA 30-year business plan has been updated, adding £68m of capital spending for future years. Funding comprises £31m from Major Repairs Reserve, £6m revenue contribution, and £31m additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Significant additions to planned HRA investment suggest material changes in housing renewal requirements; the funding split indicates increased future debt service.
findings.figures: £68m addition; £31m Major Repairs Reserve, £6m revenue, £31m borrowing
findings.quote: £68m HRA capital budget has been added to the Capital Programme in future years to align with the HRA business plan.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme July Council 2026
findings.headline: Total capital programme borrowing reaches £293.2m, with significant HRA increase to £241.7m
findings.detail: The updated capital programme is funded by £293.2m of prudential borrowing (£241.7m HRA, £51.5m GF). This represents a substantial increase requiring review as part of the Treasury Management Strategy update.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on borrowing increases debt service costs and constrains future spending flexibility; it signals substantial refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £293.2m total external borrowing; £241.7m HRA; £51.5m GF
findings.quote: The agreed budget forecast £293.2m of external borrowing to deliver the current programme, meaning that the decisions within this report would not breach the agreed Treasury Management Strategy (TMS)

findings.detail: The capital programme includes £95.8m for three Building for Lewisham schemes (Thomas Lane Yard, Achilles Phases 1&2). This is contingent on completing the procurement of a Strategic Partner.
findings.matters: A major capital commitment is conditional on procurement success; delays or failure would impact delivery timeline and borrowing profile.
findings.figures: £95.8m budget for three schemes
findings.quote: A key delivery mechanism is the conclusion of the procurement of a Strategic Partner. This has resulted in the inclusion of the programme and the £95.8m budget needed for the first schemes to be delivered under this arrangement.

findings.headline: £775.73m GLA affordable housing grant bid outcome pending; £169.5m programme impact if successful
findings.detail: Lewisham has bid to the Greater London Authority for £775.73m in grant to deliver 3,070 homes. The outcome is not yet known, but if successful would add £169.5m of investment (including £51m additional borrowing) over four years.
findings.matters: A material portion of the programme (22% of the increase) depends on uncertain external funding; non-award creates a significant shortfall requiring reallocation.
findings.figures: £775.73m grant bid; £169,516,311 programme increase if successful; £50,991,293 additional borrowing implied
findings.quote: Whilst we are yet to hear the outcome from this and seek Mayor and Cabinet approval to accept the grant, if successful this could increase the programme over the next four years by £169,516,311 including additional associated borrowing of £50,991,293.

findings.headline: £10m contingency budget for urgent unforeseen works funded from reserves in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Council has included a £10m contingency for urgent capital works that cannot be forecast in advance, to be funded from reserves. Future funding will be addressed in the 2027/28 budget setting process.
findings.matters: Creating a contingency from reserves indicates anticipated urgent pressures the council cannot forecast, reducing available liquidity.
findings.figures: £10m contingency; funded from reserves 2026/27
findings.quote: The £10m, if needed, will be funded from reserves in 2026/27, and its future funding will be addressed as part of the 2027/28 budget setting process.

findings.detail: The Council's 2025/26 capital programme delivered £139.4m against a budget of £178.1m. HRA slippage was particularly acute at £30.4m against an £81.5m budget, indicating significant execution challenges in housing delivery.
findings.matters: Persistent slippage indicates execution risk and capacity constraints in programme delivery, affecting forecast reliability and delivery capability.
findings.figures: £178.1m budget vs £139.4m outturn (£38.7m variance); HRA £81.5m budget vs £51.2m outturn (£30.4m variance)

findings.paper_title: 6, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Plan 2025-26 (KPMG) - London Borough of Lewisham - 25-26 Audit Plan
findings.headline: New Triennial Pension Valuation at 31 March 2025 likely to materially revise benefit liability and asset ceiling
findings.detail: Post-retirement benefit valuation involves high estimation uncertainty. New Triennial Valuation at 31 March 2025 will re-base actuarial models for actual scheme experience since 2022, potentially resulting in material corrections to defined benefit obligation, asset valuations, and asset ceiling assessment. Will also update contribution rates.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities typically material to council balance sheets. Changes in actuarial assumptions (discount rate, inflation, mortality) based on triennial data could significantly affect reported financial position and future contribution requirements.
findings.figures: Material enough to trigger risk assessment; specific impact not yet quantified
findings.quote: The actuary will take account of the results of the new Triennial Valuation as at 31 March 2025 for accounting at 31 March 2026. This means re-basing their estimate models to allow for actual experience since 2022, which could result in corrections to the defined benefit obligation and asset valuations this year.

findings.paper_title: 6, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Plan 2025-26 (KPMG) - London Borough of Lewisham - 25-26 Audit Plan
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage observed in prior years continues to be monitored, with substantial HRA proportion affected
findings.detail: Authority delivers significant capital programme with substantial proportion relating to Housing Revenue Account. Slippage and reprofiling of capital expenditure has been observed in prior years and continues to be monitored as part of budget management processes.
findings.matters: Capital slippage indicates budget management discipline issues and affects timing of resource deployment and financing requirements. HRA capital critical to housing maintenance; slippage defers essential investment.
findings.figures: Pattern observed in prior years; continuing but not quantified
findings.quote: The Authority continues to deliver a significant capital programme, with a substantial proportion relating to the Housing Revenue Account. Slippage and reprofiling of capital expenditure has been observed in prior years and continues to be monitored as part of the Authority's budget management processes.

findings.paper_title: 6, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Plan 2025-26 (KPMG) - London Borough of Lewisham - 25-26 Audit Plan
findings.headline: Decentralised year-end accruals processing creates identified control risk over expenditure recognition
findings.detail: Directorate structure and decentralised approach to processing year-end accruals creates risk of error in expenditure recognition. Auditors identified this as a distinct risk requiring specific test procedures on invoice timing and accruals completeness.
findings.matters: Accruals are subjective and error-prone. Distributed processing without centralised control creates incompleteness and misstatement risk, particularly where manual journals allocate costs between funds.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: We have retained a risk of error due to the directorate structure of the Authority and the decentralised approach to processing year-end accruals.

findings.paper_title: 6, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Plan 2025-26 (KPMG) - London Borough of Lewisham - 25-26 Audit Plan
findings.headline: Council dwellings valued at £1.5bn face material valuation risk from beacon property selection and indexation methods
findings.detail: Council dwellings are the largest component of land and buildings at £1.5bn of £2.8bn total (31 March 2025). The Authority uses a rolling five-year beacon revaluation model with 20% formally revalued annually and remainder indexed. Auditors identified significant risk that beacon selection errors, comparability judgements, or indexation methods could materially misstate overall valuation.
findings.matters: Council dwellings represent 54% of land and buildings balance; valuation errors at this scale could materially misstate balance sheet. Critical asset class for social housing councils.
findings.figures: £1.5bn of £2.8bn land and buildings; 20% of stock formally revalued annually
findings.quote: Council dwellings are the largest component of the Authority's land and buildings balance (£1.5bn of £2.8bn at 31 March 2025), so errors in a small number of beacons could materially impact the overall valuation.

findings.paper_title: 6, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Plan 2025-26 (KPMG) - London Borough of Lewisham - 25-26 Audit Plan
findings.headline: HRA reserves faced acute pressure in FY24, recovered partially via FY25 prior year adjustment, face ongoing difficulties in FY26
findings.detail: Lewisham's Housing Revenue Account experienced significant reserve pressure that was acute in FY24. A prior year adjustment in FY25 released funds to the HRA and improved the reserves position. The HRA continues to face financial pressures in FY26, though at reduced stress level compared to FY24.
findings.matters: HRA reserve strength is a critical credit indicator. History of acute stress with ongoing difficulties signals management challenges and potential housing service sustainability risk, relevant to both lender credit assessment and council financial direction.
findings.figures: FY24: acute; FY25: prior year adjustment released funds; FY26: ongoing pressures but reduced
findings.quote: In prior years, the Authority's HRA reserves were subject to significant pressure, with the most acute position arising in FY24. During FY25, a prior year adjustment was identified which resulted in a release of funds to the HRA and improved the reserves position. While the HRA remains subject to ongoing financial pressures in FY26, the level of stress is reduced compared with earlier years.

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 11/12/2025 Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Housing contractor management has been weak; in-house workforce productivity rising from 2 to 5 jobs per day
findings.detail: The Council identifies contractor power imbalance as a root cause of control weakness. In-house workforce productivity has increased from two jobs per day to nearly five. The Council is strengthening procurement processes to improve competition and value for money.
findings.matters: Over-reliance on contractors and weak contract management suggest poor value for money historically. While the productivity improvement is positive, it indicates the Council is still in operational recovery post-insourcing.
findings.figures: Productivity increased from 2 to 5 jobs per day
findings.quote: Weak contract management has been a root issue, with too much power resting with contractors. Improvements in the in-house workforce, whose productivity has risen from two jobs per day to nearly five, and procurement processes are underway to strengthen competition and value for money.

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 11/12/2025 Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Housing Management System lacks integration with critical systems and relies on manual workarounds
findings.detail: The new Housing Management System (launched December 2023) is now functional but a "major risk remains due to lack of integration with other key systems such as True Compliance and repairs management." Interim controls and manual workarounds ensure accuracy, but the Council acknowledges that "even small mismatches undermine assurance."
findings.matters: Poor system integration increases data quality risk and creates ongoing operational drag through manual workarounds. For a housing-intensive council, inaccurate housing data undermines both compliance assurance and financial planning reliability.
findings.figures: System launched December 2023; gaps with True Compliance and repairs management systems
findings.quote: While the system is now functional, a major risk remains due to lack of integration with other key systems such as True Compliance and repairs management. Interim controls and manual workarounds are in place to ensure accuracy, as even small mismatches undermine assurance.

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 11/12/2025 Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: 2,200 overdue fire risk actions remain in housing, particularly flat entrance doors in high-rise buildings
findings.detail: The Council has 2,200 remaining fire risk actions being prioritised by building risk and tenure. High-rise buildings require regulator gateway processes. Contractors are surveying doors, with manufacturing taking around eight weeks before fitting. The Council notes "Timelines are longer than desired but necessary to ensure compliance and avoid past mistakes."
findings.matters: Fire safety compliance in social housing is a regulatory priority. A backlog of 2,200 actions, combined with the statement about past mistakes, indicates both current non-compliance and a history of fire safety failures. Extended timelines suggest capital work will be drawn out.
findings.figures: 2,200 remaining overdue fire risk actions; manufacturing takes around eight weeks
findings.quote: The remaining 2,200 overdue fire risk actions, particularly flat entrance doors (FEDs), are being prioritised based on building risk and tenure... Timelines are longer than desired but necessary to ensure compliance and avoid past mistakes.

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 11/12/2025 Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Housing regulator compliance gap: mock inspection scored C2/C3 when C1 is required
findings.detail: A mock inspection in August 2025 suggested a rating of C2/C3, but the Council must achieve C1 for compliance. The Council acknowledges that 75–90% of inspection outcomes depend on governance and reporting, and that "root causes" must be addressed to reach the required standard. The Council is supported by a two-year Housing Transformation Programme.
findings.matters: A housing regulator compliance failure could trigger enforcement action and correction requirements. For a council with significant housing stock, this represents active regulatory risk and potential operational and financial consequences.
findings.figures: C2/C3 mock rating vs C1 required; 75–90% of outcomes depend on governance and reporting
findings.quote: The mock inspection verbally suggested a rating of C2/C3, but the goal remains C1, which requires addressing root causes.

findings.paper_title: 11, Internal Audit Plan 2026-27
findings.headline: The audit function's contingency budget for unplanned work is more constrained than in previous years.
findings.detail: The council has 700 inhouse audit days to deliver 34 planned engagements. If additional audits emerge during the year, external audit support is available but the contingency budget is explicitly stated as 'limited when compared to previous years' budgets'. This directly constrains the council's ability to respond to unexpected control issues that fall outside the plan.
findings.matters: A shrinking audit contingency reduces the council's flexibility to investigate emerging control weaknesses or unexpected risks mid-year, indicating budget pressure on the governance function.
findings.figures: 700 available inhouse audit days for 34 planned engagements; contingency budget reduced compared to prior years
findings.quote: If there are additions to the plan during the year a small contingency exists that would allow the use of external support, however, this contingency is limited when compared to previous years' budgets, and therefore additional and amendments to the plan will have to be considered carefully based on risk.

findings.paper_title: 10a, Annual Internal Audit Report - Appendix A Internal Audit summaries
findings.headline: Enterprise Risk Management lacks a formally approved risk appetite, limiting the Council's ability to define acceptable risk levels
findings.detail: The Enterprise Risk Management audit found Moderate/Limited assurance. The Council has established risk governance frameworks but does not have a formally approved risk appetite statement. Risk management processes are applied inconsistently across directorates, with variability in risk identification, scoring, and training coverage.
findings.matters: Without a defined risk appetite, the council cannot consistently prioritise capital, borrowing, or savings decisions; inconsistent risk application across directorates suggests uneven financial decision-making quality
findings.figures: 1 High Severity finding; 5 Medium Severity findings in Enterprise Risk Management
findings.quote: the Council does not yet have a formally approved risk appetite, which reduces the ability to define and communicate acceptable levels of risk

findings.paper_title: 10a, Annual Internal Audit Report - Appendix A Internal Audit summaries
findings.headline: RIDDOR reports not submitted to the HSE within set timescales under Health and Safety statutory duties
findings.detail: The Corporate Health and Safety audit found Limited assurance over the effectiveness of controls despite Substantial assurance over design. Incident records are not being completed or closed promptly, and there is evidence of failures to report to the HSE within statutory timescales under the Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations (RIDDOR).
findings.matters: Failure to report RIDDOR incidents exposes the council to enforcement action and potential fines from the HSE, and indicates a gap between documented processes and actual compliance execution
findings.figures: 2 High Severity findings identified in Corporate H&S
findings.quote: RIDDOR reports not submitted to the HSE within set timescales.

findings.paper_title: 5c Audit and Risk Committee - External Audit Update - App C - Update on 2024-25 and Prior year Recommendations – Pension Fund
findings.headline: Pension membership reconciliation was incomplete; auditors re-raised the finding because active members were not reconciled, only pensioners.
findings.detail: The 2023/24 audit found no formal member reconciliation was performed. Though the council reconciled pensioners by March 2025, the external auditor re-raised the original recommendation because it required both active and pensioner members to be reconciled. The council has now completed full reconciliation for both groups as part of 2025/26 closing.
findings.matters: The accuracy of pension fund membership directly affects the valuation of pension liabilities, a material balance sheet item for the council.
findings.figures: Reconciliation completed for both pensioner and active members in 2025/26 (previously only pensioners reconciled in 2024/25)
findings.quote: the original recommendation included active members, which the council did not reconcile, and therefore we have re-raised this

findings.paper_title: 5bAudit and Risk Committee - 25-06-26 - External Audit Update - Appendix B - Update on 2024-25 Recommendations - Main Accounts
findings.headline: System access control weakness: leaver accounts not disabled timely (now remediated)
findings.detail: Auditors identified one instance where an Oracle account for a departing employee was not disabled promptly after departure, and management could not independently verify system logs. The council has remediated by implementing automatic account disablement within one business day of termination and daily monitoring by IT.
findings.matters: Untimely revocation of financial system access creates risk of unauthorized access or data breach by former employees
findings.figures: One instance identified; remediation completed April 2026
findings.quote: we identified one instance where a leaver's user account within the Oracle system was not disabled in a timely manner after the employee's departure.

findings.paper_title: 5bAudit and Risk Committee - 25-06-26 - External Audit Update - Appendix B - Update on 2024-25 Recommendations - Main Accounts
findings.headline: Income Management system lacks automated validation for manual income code posting; remediation ongoing through Summer 2026
findings.detail: Audit identified that manual selection of income codes to transactions is not automatically validated, increasing risk of human error. One instance of incorrect coding was identified and corrected. Council is working with system provider Access Group to implement automated matching rules, due Summer 2026.
findings.matters: Weak controls over income coding increase risk of misstatement of revenue allocation and expense classification in financial statements
findings.figures: One instance identified; financial impact immaterial; remediation due Summer 2026
findings.quote: During testing of the Income Management system, we noted that manual inputs are required to assign income codes to transactions. These codes are not automatically validated, increasing the potential for human error, such as selecting incorrect codes or misallocating income between cost centres.

findings.paper_title: 5a, Audit and Risk Committee - 25-06-26 - External Audit Update - Appendix A - Update on 2024-25 Recommendations - VfM
findings.headline: Council shifting repairs delivery model to increase in-house operations versus contractor-managed work
findings.detail: The council has deliberately shifted its repairs model to increase the proportion of in-house repairs relative to contractor delivery, with new governance around contractor performance tracking and challenge meetings.
findings.matters: This operational restructuring has staffing, cost, and capacity implications that affect service sustainability and budget sustainability
findings.figures: No quantified targets provided
findings.quote: There has been a shift in the proportion of in-house repairs vs contractors to increase in-house repairs and the Authority has an action to evidence minutes of contractor meetings and challenge to contractors on performance.

findings.paper_title: 5a, Audit and Risk Committee - 25-06-26 - External Audit Update - Appendix A - Update on 2024-25 Recommendations - VfM
findings.headline: New repairs system implementation scheduled for November 2025 to address communication and performance gaps
findings.detail: The council is implementing a new repairs system in November 2025 intended to improve resident communication. Total Mobile has already been deployed to provide transparency on contractor performance and gather resident feedback to reduce complaints early in the repair journey.
findings.matters: Capital system investment and operational restructuring represents resource commitment and potential service disruption risk during implementation
findings.figures: November 2025 planned implementation date
findings.quote: The planned implementation of the new repairs system in November 2025 is hoped to improve communication with residents

findings.paper_title: 5a, Audit and Risk Committee - 25-06-26 - External Audit Update - Appendix A - Update on 2024-25 Recommendations - VfM
findings.headline: Housing Ombudsman special investigation found five systemic service failures requiring council remediation under regulatory oversight
findings.detail: An investigation into cases determined between July and October 2024 identified five emerging themes: hazards, communication with residents, contract management, knowledge and information management, and systems. The council acknowledges the significant impact of these failures on residents. Remediation is being tracked through monthly monitoring meetings with the Regulator of Social Housing and incorporated into the Housing Improvement Plan.
findings.matters: Significant operational and governance failures in a major council service indicate control weaknesses and place the council under regulatory supervision, which affects borrowing risk and management capability
findings.figures: Five emerging themes identified; investigation period July-October 2024
findings.quote: This report considered cases which were determined between July and October 2024 and had five emerging themes including hazards, communication with residents, contract management, knowledge and information management and systems.

findings.paper_title: 5, Audit and Risk Committee - 25-06-26 - External Audit Update
findings.headline: Pension Fund audit recommendation from prior years not resolved after full 2024/25 financial year
findings.detail: One pension fund audit recommendation carried forward from prior years was not fully addressed during 2024/25, prompting KPMG to re-issue it in the 2024/25 Audit Findings Report. This indicates an audit issue persisting across multiple cycles.
findings.matters: Multi-year unresolved audit findings suggest control weaknesses that the council is struggling to remediate; pension fund issues affect reported liabilities and the council's financial position
findings.figures: one prior year pension fund recommendation not fully addressed
findings.quote: For the Pension Fund there is one prior year recommendation that was not fully addressed during 2024/25 therefore KPMG re-issued this as part of the Audit Findings Report (ISA260 report)

findings.paper_title: 5, Audit and Risk Committee - 25-06-26 - External Audit Update
findings.headline: Priority one audit finding identified in 2024/25 external audit requires implementation
findings.detail: The 2024/25 external audit by KPMG identified six new recommendations for the council, including one priority one item affecting the main accounts. These were accepted by management and added to an action tracker for monitoring, but the paper does not detail what control weakness or financial issue triggered the priority one rating.
findings.matters: Priority one audit findings indicate significant control weaknesses or financial statement issues that require prompt remediation; lenders assess councils' control environments and accounting reliability
findings.figures: one priority one, two priority two and one priority three for main accounts; one priority two for Pension Fund; one priority two for Value for Money
findings.quote: six new recommendations for the Council as a result of issues identified during the course of the 2024/25 audit (four for the main accounts (one priority one, two priority two and one priority three), one for the Pension Fund accounts (priority two) and one for Value for Money (priority two))

findings.paper_title: 10, Annual Internal Audit Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: 43 high-severity audit findings remain unresolved and carried forward to 2026-27
findings.detail: Of 58 high-severity audit findings open during the year, only 15 were completed with 43 carried forward unresolved. While the overall completion rate reaches 92% for recently-due items, the 43 unresolved high-severity items indicate the council is not keeping pace with control remediation despite reported responsiveness.
findings.matters: A large backlog of unresolved high-severity findings suggests constrained execution capacity or prioritization issues in addressing identified control defects, which could accumulate over time.
findings.figures: 43 high-severity findings carried forward incomplete; 15 of 58 high-severity findings completed in-year; 57% overall completion rate (92% excluding newly-due items)
findings.quote: The overall completion percentage for actions open during the year is 57%. Excluding these issues, the percentage of issues implemented is 92%.

findings.paper_title: 8, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Draft Value for Money Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Only 42% of corporate performance metrics on or above target; 58% in 'working to improve' or 'no target' status
findings.detail: The Council's corporate performance dashboard across eight priority areas shows only 42% of KPIs at 'Almost at target' or 'On or above target' as at 2025/26 Q2, with 58% in 'Working to improve' or 'No target'. This indicates operational underperformance across the board.
findings.matters: Low metric achievement signals management capacity constraints or systemic operational challenges that may impair the council's ability to deliver savings or operational improvements
findings.figures: 58% at 'Working to improve' or 'No target'; 42% at 'Almost at target' or 'On or above target' as at 2025/26 Q2

findings.paper_title: 8, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Draft Value for Money Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Housing compliance work ongoing following 2023-24 self-referral to Regulator, with 2,500 damp and mould cases and validation gaps
findings.detail: Lewisham self-referred to the Regulator of Social Housing following non-compliance with statutory requirements in 2023-24 and commissioned improvement plans. Recent survey activity (c.1,400 additional surveys) remains subject to validation, limiting confirmation of accurate Decent Homes position. Operational pressures include c.2,500 damp and mould cases and c.860 disrepair cases. IT systems are "not designed for current regulatory requirements, increasing reliance on manual processes."
findings.matters: Housing compliance failures and backlogs in damp, mould and disrepair signal regulatory risk and potential future capital/revenue pressure; IT system gaps compound delivery risk
findings.figures: c.1,200 PFI properties (10% of 13,500 total); c.1,400 recent surveys still subject to validation; c.2,500 damp and mould cases; c.860 disrepair cases
findings.quote: operational pressures remain high, with c.2,500 damp and mould cases and c.860 disrepair cases, placing strain on data capture, monitoring, and compliance tracking. These challenges are compounded by IT systems not designed for current regulatory requirements, increasing reliance on manual processes

findings.paper_title: 8, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Draft Value for Money Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Children's services overspending by £5.9m and Adult Social Care by £3.2m, driven by placement costs and care complexity
findings.detail: Children and Young People services report a £5.9m overspend largely driven by £6.9m pressures in Family Help and Care linked to placement, accommodation and contact costs. Adult Social Care reports a £3.2m overspend driven by increasing complexity of need, higher care package costs and increased hospital discharge activity. The paper notes these are "actively managed through forecasting, performance monitoring and panel oversight" but pressures remain.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in demand-led social care suggest structural cost drivers that may not be addressable through short-term savings and create risk to medium-term budget balance
findings.figures: Children's £5.9m overspend (with £6.9m within Family Help and Care); Adult Social Care £3.2m overspend
findings.quote: Children and Young People reporting a £5.9m overspend (largely driven by £6.9m pressures in Family Help and Care linked to placement, accommodation and contact costs) and Adult Social Care reporting a £3.2m overspend, driven by increasing complexity of need, higher care package costs and increased hospital discharge activity

findings.paper_title: 8, Audit and Risk Committee 25-06-26 - External Audit Draft Value for Money Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Council budget relies on £21.7m reserves and requires £30m savings delivery by 2026/27 to address over-reliance
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget allocated £42.8m to pressures to address a £37.2m prior-year overspend. The auditors note the budget "still relies on c.£21.7m of reserves, requiring accelerated savings delivery to ensure more medium-term financial sustainability." Savings of c.£30m must be identified during 2025/26 and implemented by 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can balance future budgets without drawing reserves, and whether the £30m savings target is credible given persistent demand pressures
findings.figures: £21.7m reserves used, £30m savings required, £37.2m prior-year overspend, £42.8m allocated to 2025/26 pressures
findings.quote: the budget still relies on c.£21.7m of reserves, requiring accelerated savings delivery to ensure more medium-term financial sustainability

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 18/12/2025 Pensions Investment Committee
findings.headline: Risk of losing pension investment policy autonomy if Lewisham misses 31 March deadline
findings.detail: Lewisham must finalize its Funding Strategy Statement, Investment Strategy Statement, and Responsible Investment policies by 31 March 2026. If these are not complete by that date, the London CIV will be required to set them on behalf of the council.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would be concerned about losing control over pension investment strategy. Having a third party set investment policies carries risk to returns and strategic alignment.
findings.figures: 31 March 2026
findings.quote: However, if Lewisham did not finalise its own policies by 31 March, CIV would be required to set them.

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 18/12/2025 Pensions Investment Committee
findings.headline: Structural barrier to filling new Senior LGPS Officer statutory role
findings.detail: The council separates pension administration and investment across two different heads of finance, both of whom are excluded from the new Senior LGPS Officer role created by LGPS reform. This structural separation makes identifying a suitable candidate difficult. The cost implications of the new role are also not yet clear.
findings.matters: A finance director needs critical pension roles filled to manage compliance and investment. A lender needs to know if the council's finance function faces staffing gaps for key statutory positions.
findings.quote: The Council currently separates pension administration and investment across two heads of finance—both reporting to senior officers who are themselves excluded from taking on this new role—which made identifying a suitable candidate difficult. The cost implications were not yet clear.

findings.paper_title: 5. Investment Strategy Statement - Cover Report Final
findings.headline: Concentration of investment management to LCIV from April 2026 introduces reliance on single manager during fund maturation
findings.detail: The government-mandated transition consolidates all investment advice, asset oversight and manager monitoring into the London Collective Investment Vehicle (LCIV). While intended to create efficiencies and scale, this explicitly introduces 'a new dimension of risk—namely the reliance on one primary manager' at a time when the fund faces rising cashflow demands.
findings.matters: Operational concentration during a structurally sensitive period (fund maturation) creates risk of performance impacts or operational failures that could drive contribution rate increases
findings.figures: Transition effective 1 April 2026
findings.quote: While this change introduces a new dimension of risk—namely the reliance on one primary manager—it is accompanied by enhanced governance arrangements and ongoing performance monitoring by the PIC.

findings.paper_title: 5. Investment Strategy Statement - Cover Report Final
findings.headline: Fund is entering mature phase with rising benefit outflows requiring cashflow-focused asset reallocation
findings.detail: The fund is introducing a new asset class specifically to strengthen its cashflow position as liabilities mature and benefit outflows increase. The strategic asset allocation is being adjusted with reduced equity exposure and increased income-generating allocations to handle ongoing benefit payment demands.
findings.matters: A maturing pension fund with rising benefit outflows signals potential future pressure on employer contribution rates, which directly affects the council's financial flexibility and budget headroom
findings.figures: Target local investment allocation of 1–3% of total assets; strategic asset allocation includes 'reduction in listed equity exposure, an increase in income‑generating and real asset allocations'
findings.quote: the formal introduction of a new asset class designed specifically to strengthen the Fund's cash‑flow position as it matures... a period of increasing benefit outflows

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report Y (GF) Appendices Council
findings.headline: Adult social care and housing overspending described as 'consistent' and driving higher CIPFA risk rating than peers
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly identifies 'consistent overspending in recent years through its housing and social care activities' as a driver of above-peer-average financial risk. The budget includes £5.565m of adult social care savings proposals (care home placement review, vacancy management, fee uplifts, prevention) and £2.494m from temporary accommodation cost reduction, but these are described as 'agreed' for 2026/27, implying past proposals have not yet landed.
findings.matters: Overspending described as 'consistent' and historical suggests these are structural cost drivers not one-off pressures. Savings proposals in these areas signal recognition of the problem but also suggest delivery has been difficult.
findings.figures: Adult social care savings: £5.565m agreed; Housing (temp accommodation) savings: £2.494m; described as part of £30m total agreed cuts
findings.quote: The Council faces higher levels of risk, driven by the growth in the capital programme and consistent overspending in recent years through its housing and social care activities.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report Y (GF) Appendices Council
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £20m (90% covered by government) but sustained high-needs pressure from rising SEN identification
findings.detail: The council is 'expected to be carrying a cumulative deficit into 2026/27 in the region of £20m' on the Dedicated Schools Grant. The government announced it will cover 90% (£18m), leaving the council exposed to £2m. More material is the structural cause: 'An increasing number of schools in deficit as they adjust their resourcing plans to align with falling rolls and having to meet higher staffing and contractor costs. And the specific pressures on the high needs block to meet the costs of the rising number of young people identified with Special Education Needs (SEN).'
findings.matters: While 90% of the cumulative deficit is covered, the underlying cost drivers (SEN identification and falling rolls) are structural and unlikely to reverse. This is a demand-side pressure that will need to be managed on an ongoing basis.
findings.figures: £20m cumulative DSG deficit expected into 2026/27; government covering 90% (£18m); council exposed to £2m
findings.quote: Under the temporary override accounting treatment in place to the end of 2027/28, the Council is expected to be carrying a cumulative deficit into 2026/27 in the region of £20m. To this point the government has announced it will cover 90% of this amount, relieving much of the risk to the Council's General Fund Reserves.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report Y (GF) Appendices Council
findings.headline: First PFI contract ending 2027; council preparing to refinance with PWLB borrowing while under-borrowed and managing rising debt
findings.detail: The council is 'preparing for the first PFI contract to end in 2027 and will be seeking new PWLB debt to unwind some of its under-borrowed position'. With the capital programme in delivery and reserves being drawn, 'the Council will need to borrow in line with the TMS plans to support the capital programme'. This refinancing occurs during a period of high budget pressure and is a known cliff-edge.
findings.matters: A PFI contract ending triggers refinancing at a point when the council's financial position is stressed. The timing is fixed and not negotiable; the council must have capacity to absorb the cost impact.
findings.figures: First PFI contract ends 2027; council under-borrowed; additional PWLB borrowing planned
findings.quote: The key points to note are the Council is preparing for the first PFI contract to end in 2027 and will be seeking new PWLB debt to unwind some of its under-borrowed position. With interest rates now closer to an historic average and as reserves are being drawn the Council will need to borrow in line with the TMS plans to support the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report Y (GF) Appendices Council
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review risk: government funding assumption assumes 100% council tax collection and local growth that Lewisham will not achieve
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review consolidated grants into Core Spending Power based on assumptions that councils will raise council tax by 4.99% annually and achieve full tax collection. The CFO states 'The Council is unlikely to deliver the level of base growth and will not collect 100% of the tax due. There is therefore a risk that the Council's assessed funding to need will be eroded over time.' This is a structural funding gap built into the three-year settlement.
findings.matters: The council's baseline funding is calculated on false assumptions about income. Even if it achieves all planned savings, it will fall further behind if it cannot collect 100% of tax or achieve assumed growth—a structural mismatch likely affecting all councils but noted here as a material risk.
findings.figures: Fair Funding Review assumes 100% council tax collection and base growth aligned to local plan; Lewisham stated as unlikely to deliver either
findings.quote: The Council is unlikely to deliver the level of base growth and will not collect 100% of the tax due. There is therefore a risk that the Council's assessed funding to need will be eroded over time, although this will likely be the case for all local authorities so not a specific Lewisham risk.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report Y (GF) Appendices Council
findings.headline: CIPFA financial resilience index shows Lewisham faces higher risk than London neighbours due to capital growth and consistent service overspending
findings.detail: The council's own benchmarking shows it is above the London peer group for financial risk. The CFO attributes this to 'the growth in the capital programme and consistent overspending in recent years through its housing and social care activities'. While the council currently holds reserves to manage short-term risk, the statement warns 'they must be mitigated to enable the budget plans and reserves strategy to hold in the medium term'.
findings.matters: This is an explicit acknowledgement by the council's finance officer that its financial position is weaker than comparable councils, driven by controllable operational overspending not just external pressures.
findings.figures: Lewisham rated higher risk than nearest London neighbours on CIPFA resilience index for 2024/25
findings.quote: The Council faces higher levels of risk, driven by the growth in the capital programme and consistent overspending in recent years through its housing and social care activities. At present the Council holds reserves to manage these risks in the short term but they must be mitigated to enable the budget plans and reserves strategy to hold in the medium term.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report Y (GF) Appendices Council
findings.headline: General Fund reserves depleting from £231m to forecast £174m by end 2026/27, drawn down to fund budget gap
findings.detail: The council held £231m usable reserves at the start of 2025/26. Net drawdown in 2025/26 is £10m; by end 2026/27 earmarked reserves are forecast to drop to £174m. The budget includes 'Unwinding of 2025/26 Reserves Funding: £21.895m' as a funding source. This is using reserves as a buffer against undelivered savings rather than holding them for genuine contingency.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate indicates the budget is not self-sustaining and the council is borrowing from its own reserves to bridge the gap. Lenders need to know whether the council can stabilise before reserves become critically low.
findings.figures: £231m at start 2025/26; £174m forecast end 2026/27; £21.895m reserves used for 2025/26 funding
findings.quote: On current forecasts, the General Fund in 2025/26 will drawdown a net £10m, reflecting the combined movements of using Reserves for the Budget, movements in capital programme plans, carry forward and drawdowns against Directorate plans, and levels of interest earnt on investments. On these plans, the level of earmarked Reserves at the end of 2026/27 is forecast to drop to an estimated £174m.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report Y (GF) Appendices Council
findings.headline: Capital programme carrying £34m unmitigated downside risk from three delayed regeneration schemes
findings.detail: The council acknowledges 'the potential need to write down the capital investments of at least £10m in each of the delayed schemes to regenerate Catford, move the A205 road or deliver the planned Private Rental Scheme (PRS) at Besson Street'. The CFO notes 'the risk exposure currently outweighs the secured positive contributions by £34m'. Any write-downs hit reserves directly.
findings.matters: Write-downs would deplete reserves immediately and signal delivery risk on major regeneration. For a lender, this indicates the council's capital strategy is not delivering returns as modelled.
findings.figures: At least £10m write-down risk per scheme (three schemes); overall risk exposure £34m unmitigated
findings.quote: the potential need to write down the capital investments of at least £10m in each of the delayed schemes to regenerate Catford, move the A205 road or deliver the planned Private Rental Scheme (PRS) at Besson Street. In addition, the need to progress the plans for a strategic development partner to accelerate the larger regeneration schemes. Any write downs would hit reserves.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report Y (GF) Appendices Council
findings.headline: £36m additional savings required over next two years with delivery risk concentrated in early 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has agreed £30m of budget reductions for 2026/27 but faces a further £36m savings gap to 2028/29. The CFO statement notes the council 'has a year to identify, agree and deliver plans to bring spending back in-line with the MTFS'. Officers have 'begun the work to identify the options' but savings still need to be 'agreed in advance of the 2027/28 Budget'. This puts delivery pressure on a compressed timeline.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that proposed savings are identified, costed and deliverable. Unfunded budget gaps force either service cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £30m agreed savings for 2026/27; £36m savings still to be identified for 2027/28-2028/29 period
findings.quote: new savings proposals for £36m of budget reductions need to be agreed in 2026/27 to address the budget gap to 2028/29 arising from service pressures and the impact of the CSR and fair funding reforms

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report W (Capital) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Council's capital strategy constrained by 'significant reduction in financial resources' requiring reliance on external funding
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states that 'the council's ability to meet capital expenditure priorities are constrained by a significant reduction in financial resources' and must 'rely on internal capital resources including borrowing or, increasingly, external funds, such as grants'.
findings.matters: Structural resource constraint underpins entire capital strategy; increasing reliance on competitive external funding (grants) rather than predictable revenue sources creates delivery uncertainty.
findings.figures: Total capital strategy 2026-2045: £1,833.4m
findings.quote: Underlying the Capital Strategy is the recognition that the council's ability to meet capital expenditure priorities are constrained by a significant reduction in financial resources. The Council must therefore rely on internal capital resources including borrowing or, increasingly, external funds, such as grants and seek ways in which all investment decisions, relating to either single schemes or programmes, are financially self-sustaining or generating positive returns.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report W (Capital) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Catford regeneration requires net Council investment of £14-27m for first two phases alone
findings.detail: The council is pursuing regeneration of Catford town centre with potential for 2,700 new homes, but the delivery strategy indicates 'a significant capital cost to the Council'. Phase 1 requires 'net investment by the Council of over £14m' and Phase 2 requires 'net investment of over £27m', with the full programme expected to take 15-20 years.
findings.matters: Substantial ongoing capital commitment with extended delivery timescale; dependent on council co-investment alongside private development; significant risk if market conditions deteriorate.
findings.figures: £14m+ Phase 1; £27m+ Phase 2; 2,700 new homes target; 15-20 year delivery programme; Phases 4-6 would add further costs
findings.quote: The delivery strategy indicates a significant capital cost to the Council of participating in development, depending on the form of delivery structure and the extent of control desired by the Council. The central assumption in the strategy indicates a net investment by the Council of over £14m to enable the delivery of phase 1 sites and a net investment of over £27m to enable the development of phase 2 sites.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report W (Capital) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Hostels requiring £4.71m to meet decent homes standard, with back-office providers withdrawing management support
findings.detail: The council operates 11 temporary accommodation schemes with 50 households. Assessment identified 'decent homes works' needed across all sites with an estimated cost of £4.71m over 5 years. The driver is that 'service providers who have been managing some of the stock on the Council's behalf have changed their management model to limit their liability, pushing these back onto the Council.'
findings.matters: Forced assumption of management liability due to contractor withdrawal; underinvestment in asset base requiring catch-up spending; additional unfunded capital pressure.
findings.figures: 11 schemes; 50 households accommodated; £4.71m required over 5 years; costs front-loaded due to condition of larger schemes
findings.quote: In addition to this, service providers who have been managing some of the stock on the Council's behalf have changed their management model to limit their liability, pushing these back onto the Council.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report W (Capital) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Adult social care cost pressures continuing and growing, particularly for out-of-borough placements
findings.detail: The council notes that 'levels of need within the Adult Social Care system have increased and that trajectory is set to continue. Care placements, particularly those out of Borough and commissioned in the private sector are a significant driver of the Council's budget pressures.' The strategy commits to reviewing capital investments in housing and care infrastructure to mitigate these costs, but scale of need is driving outcomes.
findings.matters: Demographic and need-driven cost growth in ASC is a direct pressure on revenue budget; council is using capital to try to mitigate revenue pressures, suggesting revenue budget is severely constrained.
findings.figures: Provisional £15m assumed for asset modernisation; £8m for Ladywell Day Centre refurbishment; further unquantified investment needed
findings.quote: Further, levels of need within the Adult Social Care system have increased and that trajectory is set to continue. Care placements, particularly those out of Borough and commissioned in the private sector are a significant driver of the Council's budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report W (Capital) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation capital programme is essentially revenue spend masquerading as capital investment
findings.detail: The council is committing £105 million through July 2026 to purchase and refurbish up to 300 homes for temporary accommodation, with the strategy assuming 'continued levels of TA housing delivery in the period up to 2030'. The stated rationale is 'making savings or cost avoidance through reducing the Council reliance on short term and nightly paid accommodation', meaning the investment is justified by lower revenue costs, not income generation.
findings.matters: Consuming significant capital reserves to address what is fundamentally a revenue budget problem (homelessness/temporary accommodation costs); this shifts financial burden from revenue to capital and may constrain other investments.
findings.figures: £105m budget to July 2026; target of 300 homes; 100 homes purchased by January 2025; continued delivery assumed through 2030
findings.quote: The Housing Acquisition Programme (HAP) has a budget of up to £105 million to July 2026, to purchase and refurbish up to 300 homes, to be used for those who qualify for Temporary Accommodation. Its focus is on delivering high quality housing whilst making savings or cost avoidance through the reducing the Council reliance on short term and nightly paid accommodation.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report W (Capital) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Council is currently forecasting an overspend and will need to pause or abort capital schemes
findings.detail: The document explicitly states that the council may need to make additional savings, meaning certain capital schemes may need to be paused or aborted. This risk 'may become more prevalent as the Council is currently forecasting an overspend, and therefore will look to make savings to combat this.'
findings.matters: Current overspend position combined with capital programme overcommitment signals budget management stress and increased risk of scheme delays or cancellation.
findings.figures: Multiple schemes in £1.8bn capital strategy at risk
findings.quote: The Council may need to make additional savings meaning certain schemes may need to be paused/aborted. This risk may become more prevalent as the Council is currently forecasting an overspend, and therefore will look to make savings to combat this.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report W (Capital) Appendix Council
findings.headline: School decarbonisation cost of £135m currently unfunded
findings.detail: The council estimates the cost to fully decarbonise 53 schools and education facilities is approximately £135 million and is currently unfunded. The council is attempting to secure this through competitive Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme grants with match funding from annual DfE grants, which puts other building condition works under pressure.
findings.matters: This is an unfunded liability that will either require future borrowing or result in deferred maintenance across the school estate; climate commitments may force acceleration regardless of funding.
findings.figures: £135m estimated cost; 53 schools; average annual DfE grant approximately £4m
findings.quote: The estimated cost to fully decarbonise 53 schools across the council's school sites and education facilities is approximately £135M and is currently unfunded.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report W (Capital) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Building for Lewisham housing programme failing viability benchmark despite higher grant rates
findings.detail: The council's main housing delivery programme has become 'increasingly difficult to maintain the programme's viability benchmark of a -£10m NPV' due to construction sector volatility, budget pressures and predicted falls in Right-to-Buy receipts following Autumn Budget 2024. The council is mitigating through partnership working, procurement for a Strategic Partner, and diversifying into shared ownership and acquisitions rather than direct build.
findings.matters: The flagship housing programme underpins the council's growth strategy and borrowing plans; viability pressures indicate either delivery will slow or costs will need to be absorbed elsewhere.
findings.figures: Over 1,000 new homes in pre-construction or pipeline; viability benchmark of -£10m NPV; nearly 350 completions delivered since 2018
findings.quote: due to ongoing volatility with the construction sector and budget pressures, despite the Council achieving higher GLA Affordable Housing Programme (AHP) grant rates, it is increasingly difficult to maintain the programme's viability benchmark of a -£10m NPV; and has been made even more difficult by the predicted fall in Right-to-Buy receipts following the Autumn Budget 2024.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report V (Climate Budget) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Leisure centre decarbonisation uncertain due to third-party management and ongoing procurement.
findings.detail: Section 5.7 notes leisure centres are managed by a third-party provider responsible for investment and maintenance, with no council capital budget allocated. A procurement exercise for a new provider was underway at the time of the report, creating uncertainty about future carbon investment despite leisure centres representing 2,085 tCO2 annually.
findings.matters: A material asset with significant emissions sits outside direct council control, creating uncertainty in achieving stated net-zero 2030 targets and potentially requiring negotiation with future service providers.
findings.figures: Leisure centre emissions 2023/24: 2,085 tCO2; estimated decarbonisation cost: £3,000,000
findings.quote: Leisure centre sites are managed by a third-party provider of leisure services, including responsibility to investment and maintenance of the buildings. As a result there is no budget for leisure centres in the capital programme although the leisure service contract includes provisions to energy efficiency and carbon reduction projects.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report V (Climate Budget) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Fleet investment constrained; council cannot afford fully electric vehicle replacement.
findings.detail: Section 5.8 notes that Mayor and Cabinet approved a fleet strategy in December 2025 with £10.7m (general fund) and £5m (HRA) over three years. However, the council can only allocate one-third of this budget to carbon savings, with the document stating it is 'not possible to fund fully electric replacement vehicles.'
findings.matters: Reveals a structural gap between stated climate ambitions and financial capacity, indicating whether the council's net-zero 2030 target is realistic or constrained by affordability.
findings.figures: Fleet capital: £10,669,859 (general fund), £5,038,861 (HRA), approved over 3 years; one-third allocated to carbon savings
findings.quote: This recognises that at present it is not possible to fund fully electric replacement vehicles.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report V (Climate Budget) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Decarbonisation funding is dependent on competitive grants with no long-term certainty.
findings.detail: Section 5.1 states the council's main funding source has been 'short-term competitive funding opportunities impacting on the ability to forecast a trajectory.' Section 5.10 notes that housing retrofit funding (£20.9m) is 'subject to achieving annual targets for grant expenditure,' creating execution risk if targets are missed.
findings.matters: Grant-dependency creates volatility in capital planning. Failure to meet targets or grant discontinuation could force the council to defer projects or draw on reserves.
findings.figures: Housing retrofit funding: £11,441,176 grant, £9,441,177 match funding (HRA), over 2026/27-2028/29
findings.quote: The main source of funding for decarbonisation work has tended to be short-term competitive funding opportunities impacting on the ability to forecast a trajectory and establish long-term plans.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report V (Climate Budget) Appendix Council
findings.headline: Estimated decarbonisation costs of £743m far exceed the budgeted spend of £44m over three years.
findings.detail: The council estimates total costs of £273m for corporate decarbonisation and £470m for council housing. Against this, the 2026/27-2028/29 capital forecast is £23.1m for corporate and £20.9m for housing, representing only 6% of the estimated need. Section 5.1 explicitly states the cost is 'significantly beyond existing budgets.'
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether the council's financial commitments are realistic and whether climate spending will require unsustainable borrowing or crowd out other essential services.
findings.figures: Estimated costs: £273,000,000 (corporate), £470,000,000 (housing). Forecast 2026/27-2028/29: £23,100,000 (corporate), £20,900,000 (housing)
findings.quote: The cost of achieving that ambition is significantly beyond existing budgets and setting year-on-year milestones for decarbonisation is difficult without long-term certainty on funding.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report X (HRA) Appendices Council
findings.headline: Final rent increase for 2026-27 remains unconfirmed, with government to announce rent convergence policy in January 2026 that could add £1-3/week
findings.detail: The minimum rent increase is set at 4.8% (£5.95/week), but the government has not yet confirmed whether rent convergence will be permitted. If approved, convergence could add £1, £2, or £3 per week to rents. The government will announce the convergence policy in January 2026. This creates planning uncertainty as the final rent increase could range from 4.8% to 7.22% depending on the government's decision.
findings.matters: The council's HRA Business Plan and income projections depend on rent increases, but the final amount remains uncertain. The difference between scenarios is material (£4.268m vs £6.420m additional income).
findings.figures: Minimum increase 4.8% (£5.95/week, £129.91 new average rent). Potential increases: +£1/week (5.61%), +£2/week (6.41%), +£3/week (7.22%). Additional income ranges from £4.268m (baseline) to £6.420m (with £3 convergence).
findings.quote: The Authority are waiting to hear from Government whether or not rent convergence - the process by which rents are 'normalised' will be permitted, which may then add an additional £1, £2, or £3 per week, which is to be confirmed in January 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Report X (HRA) Appendices Council
findings.headline: Council writing off £121,784 in former tenant arrears across 8 cases, unable to trace or collect from evicted and vulnerable tenants
findings.detail: Eight HRA arrears cases are being written off totalling £121,784. Cases include evicted tenants who could not be traced (£22,965, £18,010, £13,123); tenants who died with no estate (£11,955); and vulnerable tenants with complex circumstances. In each case the council's debt collection agency returned the case as unable to collect. Cases show tenants moving out of London, returning to prison, or becoming deceased before arrears could be recovered.
findings.matters: Shows collection challenges in the HRA, particularly with vulnerable and mobile populations. The council's debt collection efforts are returning cases as unrecoverable. This signals arrears management risk.
findings.figures: £121,783.96 in HRA arrears write-offs. Eight individual cases ranging from £10,497 to £22,967. Total write-offs across HRA and General Fund reach £468,680.
findings.quote: The Director of Resident Engagement and Services and the Head of Service Finance recommend the write off 28 debts totalling £468,680.52 across HRA and General Fund Housing.
